source.title: MoE Sparsity Begets Monosemanticity: Insights into Understanding and Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Ming-Xue Tian; Qi Zhang; Xiao-Han Wang; Jia-Jun Chai; Guo-Jun Yin; Wei Lin; Cai-Lian Chen; Qi-Min Xu; Si-Yu Wang; Yi-Sen Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study reports results about MoE expert-level monosemanticity and gives a qualitative expert-versus-neuron comparison, but it does not test neuron-pole job shares or any other listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The study treats MoE experts as analogous to SAE neurons, but its main measures (EMS, EDMS and LDS) are expert-level activation-prediction scores, not proportions of neuron poles with one or two jobs. The qualitative neuron examples do not establish such proportions. Fine-tuning results and cited findings are not results on the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study scores MoE experts, not individual neurons, by predicting expert activation from LLM explanations. It reports no share of neurons or neuron poles with one or two jobs, no InceptionV1 analysis, no attribution graphs, and no neuron-level simulation scores. The neuron comparison in Appendix A.10 / Table 8 shows only a few qualitative examples from one expert. So its results do not bear on any listed version. The expert-level findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that MoE sparsity promotes expert-level monosemanticity, that middle layers are most specialized, and that experts are either domain-specific or general. On that basis they propose EDMRS expert-selected fine-tuning, which matches full fine-tuning in-domain and better retains out-of-domain performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study generates natural-language explanations for MoE experts and uses an external LLM to predict expert activation, then scores prediction accuracy. It does not conduct the neuron-pole audit or share estimation described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported LDS varies with sparsity and layer; the paper also reports differences between general and domain-specific expert scores. It reports a qualitative change in LDS with explanation word limit in Appendix A.12.

fits_no_version.finding: Lowering MoE sparsity (more activated experts) lowers layer-average expert monosemanticity (LDS) in Qwen3-30B-A3B. Shown in a figure only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE models, higher routing sparsity is associated with higher expert-level explanation-prediction accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: LDS across depth in Qwen3-235B-A22B rises early, plateaus in the middle layers and drops near the output.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert-level monosemanticity peaks in middle layers of MoE LLMs.

fits_no_version.finding: Domain-specific EDMS is generally lower than general EMS. Both specialized and multi-domain (polysemantic) experts exist.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE experts are a mix of domain-specialized and cross-domain experts.

fits_no_version.finding: Neuron explanations inside Expert 114 describe token-level patterns (brackets, numbers, function words), while the expert's explanation describes medical textbook content.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert-level explanations are coarser and more semantic than neuron-level explanations in the same layer.

fits_no_version.finding: On one middle layer, LDS stays around 0.69–0.71 across explanation word limits of 20–100 (Table 9), with 20 words best (0.7081).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert explanation-prediction accuracy is about 0.7 and barely sensitive to explanation length.

record.peer_reviewed: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
record.problems: The claim-relevant comparison is at expert level, not neuron-pole level. The plotted LDS and EMS/EDMS results have no extractable numerical values in the supplied text. The neuron comparison is qualitative and based on examples rather than a reported share or aggregate score.
record.rows_left_out: No results from the domain fine-tuning comparisons were included because they report downstream task performance, not neuron-pole monosemanticity or a listed claim-version measure. Evaluator-correlation results were also omitted because they assess score agreement, not the listed claim.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit and no one-job, two-job or not-understood shares.
MoE results are at expert level. No neuron-pole shares are given across models or scale.
No analysis of InceptionV1 or of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No comparison of neuron interpretability shares across architectures or tools, and no vision models.
No attribution graphs or circuit tests.
Activation prediction is applied to experts, not to neuron explanations.
No neuron-level simulation scores and no share of neurons scoring well.

record.verdict_notes: The record's statement that no numerical LDS values are extractable is slightly wrong: Table 9 gives LDS values of 0.6869–0.7081 for one layer, but at expert level. Evaluator robustness is also reported: Spearman correlations of 0.815 with GPT-4o-mini, 0.774 with Qwen3.5 and 0.701 with human annotators. None of these bear on the neuron-level versions.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or estimates of one-job, two-job, or unexplained shares.
Does not measure neuron-pole shares across dense and MoE models or across model scales; its MoE measurements concern experts.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car analysis or test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
No study of InceptionV1-sized vision models, late-layer neuron interpretability shares, or architecture/tool-driven share estimates.
No attribution-graph or circuit reconstruction test using model neurons.
No test of neuron explanations against activating examples and separate firing predictions.
No automated scoring results for neuron explanations or estimate of the share of neurons with good scores.

rows.subject: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of activated experts per token and measured layer-wise LDS, defined as average expert EMS.
rows.measure: Layer-wise Decoupling Score (LDS), average expert monosemanticity
rows.note: The text says that reducing sparsity consistently and substantially decreases LDS across all evaluated layers; it says the trend holds across evaluated k values.

rows.subject: Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507

conditions.value: network depth; individual layer values not stated

rows.note: The text describes a rapid LDS increase in early layers, a high middle-layer plateau, and a sharp decline near the output.

rows.subject: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507
rows.operation_detail: Applied general and domain-specific explanation prompts and measured EMS and EDMS for experts.
rows.measure: Expert monosemanticity (EMS) and expert domain monosemanticity (EDMS)
rows.note: The text says EDMS scores are generally lower than EMS scores and reports both domain-specialized and polysemantic experts activated across multiple domains.

rows.subject: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507
rows.operation_detail: Applied the explanation framework separately to experts and neurons in a selected intermediate layer and compared the semantic granularity of the explanations.

conditions.value: randomly selected intermediate layer described as monosemantic

rows.value: Neuron explanations are described at a lower semantic level; example neuron explanations concern token fragments, numbers, and common words, while the expert explanation covers broad medical textbook content.
rows.note: This is a qualitative comparison with examples, not a measurement of how many neuron poles have one main job.

relation.reason: Only a side comparison of expert and neuron semantic granularity. It does not test, use or cite the neurons-already-clean claim.

tranche.reason: Scores MoE experts by LLM-explanation activation prediction, not neuron poles. The only neuron material (A.10, Table 8) is six qualitative example explanations, with no share or score.

source_check.notes: All four rows match the text; r1-r3 are figure-only, with no numbers. The paper names no model for the A.10 neuron examples. Its statement that dense LLMs have lower monosemanticity is an assertion, not a measurement. No verdicts are warranted.
